hints: Think about reactivity order for statement 1, thermal decomposition for statement 2, and basic oxide behaviour for statement 3.
Calcium sits above magnesium in the reactivity series, so ask yourself which metal holds on to oxygen more strongly.
Recall what a Group 2 nitrate gives on heating and what quicklime does in water, then combine the two true statements to pick the option.
walkthrough:
**Check statement 1 with the reactivity series**

Think of reduction of an oxide as taking oxygen away. A more reactive metal can steal oxygen, a less reactive one cannot.

Reactivity order: $\text{Ca} > \text{Mg}$

**Decide if magnesium reduces calcium oxide**

Because calcium is more reactive than magnesium, $\text{CaO}$ is more stable than $\text{MgO}$. Heating them together gives no reaction.

$$\text{CaO} + \text{Mg} \rightarrow \text{no reaction}$$
So statement 1 is incorrect.

**Check statement 2, heating calcium nitrate**

All Group 2 nitrates decompose on heating to the oxide plus nitrogen dioxide and oxygen. Calcium is no exception.

$$2\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2 \rightarrow 2\text{CaO} + 4\text{NO}_2 + \text{O}_2$$
So statement 2 is correct.

**Check statement 3, reaction with cold water**

Calcium oxide is basic quicklime. It reacts vigorously even with cold water to make calcium hydroxide, which is why the mixture gets hot.

$$\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$$
So statement 3 is correct. Only 2 and 3 are correct.

options.A: This option includes statement 1 as well as 2 and 3. Statement 1 is wrong because magnesium is less reactive than calcium and cannot reduce $\text{CaO}$. Students who reverse the reactivity order choose this.
options.B: This option pairs 1 and 2 only. It keeps the false statement 1 and leaves out the true statement 3. $\text{CaO}$ definitely reacts with cold water to form $\text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$, so this combination cannot be right.
options.C: Lovely, this is correct. Statement 2 is true by thermal decomposition of $\text{Ca}(\text{NO}_3)_2$ to $\text{CaO}$, and statement 3 is true by $\text{CaO} + \text{H}_2\text{O} \rightarrow \text{Ca}(\text{OH})_2$, while statement 1 is false on reactivity grounds.
options.D: This option selects statement 1 only. That is the one false statement, since a less reactive metal ($\text{Mg}$) cannot take oxygen from the oxide of a more reactive metal ($\text{Ca}$).
